beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: Nothing new yet; this is the title, and it is the right topic for my fourteen people.

beats.trigger: You can't really share an agent. You can share context, a skill, the output, or an interface.
beats.got: Sharing means handing over four specific things, not the agent itself, and the hard part is whether people actually use it.

beats.trigger: Walk in with one example where people had access to a tool or process but real use did not follow.
beats.got: Nothing new. I have an example ready: the CRM rollout nobody opened.

beats.trigger: **Redesign** for shared use: technical plan + people plan (ownership, governance, operating, accountability, propagation)
beats.got: Five verbs, and the people plan is half of it. That matches my situation, but it's still a list of outcomes.

beats.trigger: And what makes you hesitate about actually handing this to them?
beats.got: I hesitate because they'd run it and get generic output. That is already the module's point.

beats.trigger: Your teammate doesn't want your agent. They want a job done.
beats.got: I should start from my teammate's job, not from my setup. That's obvious once said, and I don't do it.

beats.trigger: does it name one teammate, their current way of doing the job, and an outcome you could observe?
beats.got: The agent interviews me about one pricing-group colleague, and I can test the result by whether it is specific. That's a usable check.

beats.trigger: Share the context. Your `memory/`, `sources/`, root instructions, and `style.md` travel. Teammates build on top.
beats.got: Shared context is a real option, and it is exactly my blocker of everyone keeping their own copy of the files.

beats.trigger: You now have the teammate's job and a candidate selected against it.
beats.got: Nothing new; it's a handoff to the next exercise.

beats.trigger: Now find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can actually absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: Next I name the one thing that will stop adoption, then plan around it.

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: Look for the obstacle that makes the others hard, not the first technical limit. That is how I would judge it before the CFO does.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: Unnamed owners show up as a visible gap instead of being papered over. That is exactly what my team does.

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure, and writes the first real-world contact to `module-7/monday.md`.
beats.got: Nothing new; it's a signpost.

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: The plans are guesses until a person touches them.

beats.trigger: what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?
beats.got: I should list what has to be true for them to drop their current way, then pick two or three tests for this week.

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: Imagining it failed gives me one named conversation and one test, which is useful, but it's a premortem and I have done those.

beats.trigger: Test the switch, not the solution.
beats.got: A four-line recap of the exercises. Nothing new.

beats.trigger: The rest of this is about the person on the other end of your plan.
beats.got: The lecture is about the receiver.

beats.trigger: A good interview finds a third outcome past speed and quality: a dependency removed, an anxiety gone, a scope widened.
beats.got: Beyond faster and better there are outcomes like removing a dependency or an anxiety. I hadn't thought about my team that way.

beats.trigger: Hand someone the agent file and they run it, get a generic answer, and quietly stop.
beats.got: Nothing new; this is the big idea again, with a good image of someone quietly stopping.

beats.trigger: Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.
beats.got: Context, boundary and checks copy easily, but somebody still has to answer for the output, and that stays with me.

beats.trigger: The two get reported as one number and they are not one thing.
beats.got: Nothing new: access versus absorption, third time in different words. The point about the single reported number is the only fresh bit.

beats.trigger: *we know more than we can tell.*
beats.got: My teammates need to recognise it from their own work. The Polanyi quote is a detour.

beats.trigger: The interface is the first piece whose shape depends on somebody whose calendar you do not control.
beats.got: The interface is where it depends on other people's time.

beats.trigger: The leadership had not done the analysis. People they trusted had.
beats.got: A good analysis can die because the decision-makers never owned it. That could happen to my pricing proposal with the CFO.

beats.trigger: Somebody they trust has to have used it first and said so.
beats.got: The switch conditions are small and concrete: it lands where they look, it's right the first time, and a trusted peer used it first.

beats.trigger: Whether they pick it up is their decision, made for their own reasons, on a Tuesday you will not be in the room for.
beats.got: Nothing new; it's the same lesson as before, just more poetic.

beats.trigger: One name. One person whose week this would change, who would tell you plainly if it did not.
beats.got: Start with one honest person, not fourteen.

beats.trigger: The agent reviews, rewrites the sharing artifact in place, and reports what changed.
beats.got: The agent sharpens my sharing file and I push back. This is routine; the edit-only-the-section tip is useful.

beats.trigger: The artifact: the sharpened sharing file itself, plus one line in your Module 7 next-step file naming the first move.
beats.got: I leave with a sharpened file and one line naming my first move.

beats.trigger: Access is easy; absorption is scarce.
beats.got: Nothing new; a recap.

beats.trigger: Test one assumption. Ask for one name. Talk to one person.
beats.got: I have homework before Module 8: run monday.md and bring back what happened.

beats.trigger: What comes back from that contact is Module 8's raw material.
beats.got: Nothing new.

take_homes: Share the context first: put our shared context files in one place the team builds on, instead of fourteen private copies.
Start from one teammate's job and what would have to be true for them to switch, not from my setup.
Find the owner for each part of the people plan. An unnamed owner means the plan isn't ready.

monday.move: Pick one person in the pricing working group, ask how they currently do the pilot-cohort brief, and test one switch assumption with a shared copy of the context files.
monday.who: One member of the pricing working group, to be named by me tonight.
monday.when: Monday morning, 30 minutes with them, then the brief re-run with fresh data by Wednesday.
monday.stop_condition: If they say they would go back to their own spreadsheet and can't tell me what would change that, I drop this candidate and look at the next one.
monday.blocker: We have no shared home for the context files, so I need IT or a teammate to agree on one folder.

misconception.why: Good prompts didn't help the colleague who quietly stopped using the agent file. What matters more is the context, the owner and the job. I still think prompt quality counts for my own work.

one_line: Good, practical module on why handing a colleague your agent doesn't work. It's repetitive in the lecture, but I got a named person and a Monday test out of it.
